# Corrections

### Second accuracy pass on drug records (slice 1), 18 November 2026

A second, independent read of drug records, one third of the corpus's drugs, starting with the approved medicines that most pages link to. Each record, its regional approval rows, dosing and side-effect rows, access notes and plain-language line was checked claim by claim against the current US label, the regulator's own pages, the trial registry and the papers cited, all read as raw text. All 232 approved medicines and tests in the slice are now done: 4,357 ledger rows, of which 322 were wrong, 178 were not supported by the source and 94 could not be re-read; the pipeline drugs follow. The most serious faults: sacituzumab govitecan's plain-language line and eight translations still described it as a bladder cancer drug two years after that approval was withdrawn; dostarlimab's one-line summary said rectal cancer disappeared in every patient, where the trial behind its 2026 approval found a sustained complete response in about half to two thirds; NHS access lines for ten medicines cited the wrong NICE appraisal or presented a terminated or negative appraisal as a recommendation; docetaxel's prostate cancer survival figures for all patients were presented as the result in high-volume disease; and sacituzumab tirumotecan was shown as having no US filing after one had gone under review. In the second batch: savolitinib was shown as not filed in the United States or Europe after applications had gone in on a trial that reported in August 2026; camizestrant's first-line trial was described as still to report after it missed its primary endpoint in September 2026; alpelisib and glofitamab were shown as approved in Japan, where neither is; capivasertib's dose reduction and blood sugar threshold and crizotinib's dose in liver impairment did not match their labels; and pegylated liposomal doxorubicin was said to replace the heart damage of ordinary doxorubicin although its label carries a boxed warning for it. In the third batch: ropeginterferon alfa-2b and aminolevulinic acid gel had each gained a US indication in 2026 that the records did not show; ciltacabtagene autoleucel was shown as recommended by NICE, which has made no recommendation, and its monitoring rules lagged the label; sugemalimab was shown as under review in the United Kingdom two years after its approval there; larotrectinib's response rate was the 75 per cent of its first 55 patients, where the current label gives 60 per cent of 339; and two companion diagnostic records credited tests with claims the FDA's list gives to other tests or to none. In the fourth batch: three European authorisations were shown as current after they had ended (tilmanocept in 2024, ibritumomab tiuxetan in 2024, palifermin in 2016); gefitinib's withdrawn 2003 US approval stood as a current row; glumetinib lacked its 2024 Japanese approval and claimed a gastric cancer phase 3 trial that does not exist; tucidinostat's melanoma trial was described as still being tested after it reported in October 2026; imlunestrant's one-line summaries said it works with abemaciclib regardless of mutation without saying that the US approval of the pair is limited to ESR1-mutated disease; and ziv-aflibercept was said to carry boxed warnings its current label no longer has. In the fifth batch: axicabtagene ciloleucel was said to cure about 40 per cent of patients in its one-line summary and translations, where the five-year trial report gives 42.6 per cent alive and 31 per cent still in response; vorasidenib was called the first targeted therapy for low-grade brain tumours, which dabrafenib with trametinib preceded in children, and was shown as under review in Japan a year after approval there; revumenib's dose-holding rule gave a QT threshold of 500 ms where the label interrupts at 480 ms; naxitamab's approval response rates were 50 and 45 per cent where the label gives 45 and 34; a blood test for bowel cancer was called the second approved by the FDA when it was the third; and FoundationOne CDx was credited with a companion claim the FDA's list does not contain. In the sixth batch: temsirolimus was said to have improved survival without relapse in childhood rhabdomyosarcoma, in its summary, one-line descriptions and eight translations, when the trial found no improvement; a lung cancer blood test (Resolution ctDx FIRST) was shown as approved after the FDA's database recorded its approval as withdrawn in June 2025; abarelix's 2005 US withdrawal was put down to allergic reactions where the maker gave economic reasons; raloxifene was said to be about as effective as tamoxifen, which held only at the first analysis; radium-223 with abiraterone was described as contraindicated without bone protection, where Europe contraindicates the combination outright; and mercaptopurine's record said gene testing is recommended before starting, where the US label advises considering it after severe bone marrow suppression. In the seventh batch: zidesamtinib was said to avoid the brain side effects of other drugs of its kind, in its summary and eight translations, where its label carries a warning for them in a quarter of patients, and its restriction to people already treated with a similar drug was missing; ravulizumab was described as still being tested after transplant when its trial had reported no significant difference in November 2026; nabilone, granisetron's slow-release injection and cinacalcet's originator brand were shown as available after being discontinued, while cinacalcet itself was wrongly shown as withdrawn in Europe; and haloperidol's first US approval was dated 1971 where the tablets were approved in 1967.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages, part two: lung, pancreatic and blood cancer subtype pages, 18 November 2026

Fourteen lung cancer subtype and stage pages with their ten trial records, eleven pancreatic cancer pages, and twenty-one blood cancer pages (acute myeloid leukaemia, myeloma, myelodysplastic syndromes, chronic lymphocytic and chronic myeloid leukaemia, myelofibrosis, polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia). 618 ledger rows, of which 96 were wrong, 66 were not supported by the source cited and 41 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: both small-cell lung cancer pages offered lurbinectedin at relapse after that indication left the US label in September 2026; three lung trials that reported in 2026 (Krascendo 1, LIBRETTO-432, DeLLphi-305) were shown as awaited or missing; the MORPHO trial of gilteritinib after transplant, which missed its primary endpoint, was written as a benefit; the smouldering myeloma page said no trial had shown a survival gain when two have; a chronic lymphocytic leukaemia triplet was shown as approved in the United States when the approval excludes it; and belantamab mafodotin was given a wider US indication than its label.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages, part two: 71 rarer cancers, 18 November 2026

The thirty cancers of the gap round (among them vulvar, testicular and anal cancer, Kaposi sarcoma, GIST, follicular and mantle cell lymphoma, the chronic myeloid diseases and the childhood solid tumours), twelve rare cancers from the NCI list (among them penile and vaginal cancer and ductal carcinoma in situ) and thirty-five subtype and setting pages. 789 ledger rows, of which 182 were wrong, 121 were not supported by the source cited and 84 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: a negative rhabdomyosarcoma trial (ARST1431) was written as positive in four places; GIST median survival was given as eight years or more where the trials report 3.9 years; retifanlimab in anal cancer was described as a survival benefit that the trial did not show; a vaginal cancer guideline was cited with the DOI of a prostate brachytherapy paper; luspatercept was listed for myelofibrosis after its phase 3 trial missed its endpoint; and BALLAD, InPACT, tabelecleucel and several nasopharyngeal treatments carried statuses that events had overtaken.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages, part two: Hodgkin lymphoma, the family pages and ten more main records, 18 November 2026

Hodgkin lymphoma and its four subtype pages; the base records of the lung cancer, breast cancer, leukaemia, biliary tract cancer, cholangiocarcinoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma pages; and mesothelioma, sarcoma, neuroendocrine tumours, neuroblastoma, brain tumours, childhood cancers, extragonadal germ cell tumour and metastatic cancer. 395 ledger rows, of which 96 were wrong, 67 were not supported by the source cited and 26 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: the RATHL trial was written as showing bleomycin could be dropped with no loss, where the paper says the result fell just short of its non-inferiority margin; tazemetostat was listed as a current sarcoma treatment after its US approval was withdrawn; the biliary page said gallbladder cancer has no approved targeted drug; the neuroblastoma page turned a two-year event-free survival figure into long-term survival of about 60 per cent; and 47 trials and 11 pipeline drugs were linked to cancers they do not study, most of them non-Hodgkin lymphoma products filed under Hodgkin lymphoma.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages, part two: the breast cancer family, 18 November 2026

The files the first half did not reach for breast cancer: the family page and its glossary, the living-with layer, the UK pathway, the surgery, radiotherapy and reconstruction layer with its trials, and the residual-disease records. 890 ledger rows, of which 73 were wrong, 97 were not supported by the source cited and 19 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: a reconstruction trial (Best-BRA) was shown as running and awaited although its registry record says it stopped after 11 of a planned 100 women; OPTIMA, inavolisib and imlunestrant were shown as awaited or in development after the trial reported and NICE published; the page said Northern Ireland publishes no breast waiting-time figures, and it does; breast cancer was called the commonest cancer in the world where GLOBOCAN 2024 ranks it second; and three trials were given the wrong denominator (INSEMA, SOUND and the MROC cohort).

### Second accuracy pass on the drug records: sixty-two more approved products, 18 November 2026

The second group of approved products in the drug records' second read: sixty-two medicines, regimens, cell therapies, imaging agents and companion tests, among them blinatumomab, brentuximab vedotin, lorlatinib, erdafitinib, tisagenlecleucel, zongertinib, isatuximab, tebentafusp and mosunetuzumab. 1,253 ledger rows, of which 107 were wrong, 82 were not supported by the source cited and 67 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: retifanlimab was said to lengthen survival in anal cancer, where the US label's interval crosses one and only the delay in progression is established; afamitresgene autoleucel carried a dose range, a response duration and a maker that the current label does not; the SP142 PD-L1 test showed US bladder and breast claims that the FDA removed in 2021 and 2023; S-1 was credited with a non-inferiority result that was a post hoc reading of a trial that missed its endpoint; and blinatumomab's 2024 approval was described more widely than its label and credited to the wrong trials. Trials shown as running had been stopped or had reported (IMpactMF, CELESTIMO, KROCUS, a ripretinib result that does not exist), and six NICE appraisal numbers were replaced, terminated or belonged to another medicine.

### Second accuracy pass on the drug records: the forty-nine most linked approved medicines, 18 November 2026

The first second read of the drug records, which had been checked once when written and not since. Forty-nine approved medicines, the most linked first, among them pembrolizumab, osimertinib, olaparib, venetoclax, ipilimumab, abemaciclib, ribociclib and enfortumab vedotin: each record, its regional approval rows, its dosing and side-effect rows and its plain-language line were read claim by claim against the current US label, the European Medicines Agency's table, NICE guidance, trial registries and the papers cited. 1,604 ledger rows, of which 140 were wrong, 95 were not supported by the source cited and 95 could not be re-read. The most serious faults were stale: trials written as awaited or running that had reported (FURVENT missed its endpoint, STAR-221 was stopped for futility, MagnetisMM-5 and the final monarchE and NATALEE survival analyses had read out), approvals granted in China in 2025 and 2026 that the records did not show, and a US application shown as under review that had never been filed. Doses were wrong against the label for ipilimumab in liver cancer, venetoclax with antifungal medicines, selinexor in myeloma and disitamab vedotin in gastric cancer. Several NICE appraisal numbers pointed at guidance that has been replaced, ended or is about another medicine. Approval years for the United Kingdom, China and Australia could often not be re-read, because those regulators' pages do not answer a script; where a row could carry a note, it says so.

### Second accuracy pass on drug records: the last forty approved medicines and tests (slice 2, sixth batch), 18 November 2026

A second, independent read of the last 40 approved medicines, vaccines and tests in this slice, from mitotane, osilodrostat and the Shield blood test to olaratumab, bexarotene, allopurinol and warfarin. 437 claims were checked: 31 were wrong, 26 were not supported by the source cited and 9 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: the Shield record described a mechanism the FDA replaced with a methylation-only version in July 2026 and called it the first approved blood test for bowel cancer screening, which Epi proColon was in 2016; olaratumab's withdrawal was dated 2019 worldwide, where the US withdrawal was February 2020, and the antibody was filed under kinase inhibitors; bexarotene gel was given the capsules' indication; osilodrostat's US indication had not been widened to Cushing's syndrome as it was in April 2025; a database link on uracil mustard led to an antibiotic; and racotumomab's survival result was given without saying its phase 3 trial has reported nothing since 2016.

| Date | Entity | What was wrong | How found | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-11-18 | [Shield](/drugs/shield/) | The record said Shield reads cell-free DNA for methylation, fragmentation and mutation signals. On 22 July 2026 the FDA approved a change that makes the test methylation-only, removing the fragmentomic and somatic components. | FDA premarket approval database, P230009 supplement S010 (decision 22 July 2026), read from the openFDA device API and the FDA page as raw text. | Mechanism, summary, mechanism steps and regulatory timeline now give the methylation-only workflow and the date of the change. |
| 2026-11-18 | [Shield](/drugs/shield/) | The record, its one-line summary and its plain line called Shield "the first FDA-approved blood test for colorectal cancer screening". The FDA approved an earlier blood test, Epi proColon, on 12 April 2016 for average-risk adults who had been offered other screening and had not completed it. Guardant's own claim is narrower: the first blood test approved as a primary screening option. The record also said the test now optionally reports other cancers; Guardant's site says the multi-cancer report is not part of the FDA-approved test. | FDA premarket approval records P130001 (Epi proColon) and P230009 (Shield) from the openFDA device API; Guardant's release of 29 July 2024 (archived copy) and shieldbloodtest.com, read as raw text. | "First" is now attributed to Guardant with its qualifier, the earlier test is named, and the multi-cancer sentence says what the company's site says. |
| 2026-11-18 | [Shield](/drugs/shield/) | The approval was dated 29 July 2024, which is the day Guardant announced it; the FDA decision date is 26 July 2024. The record also said Medicare covers Shield under a "2024" coverage rule: the rule (NCD 210.3) has covered qualifying blood-based tests since January 2021, and that Shield meets it is Guardant's statement. | FDA premarket approval P230009 (decision date 07/26/2024); CMS national coverage determination 210.3 read as raw HTML; Guardant release of 29 July 2024 (archived). | Approval date corrected; the Medicare sentence now gives the rule's terms (once every three years, age 45 to 85, average risk) and attributes Shield's eligibility to the company. |
| 2026-11-18 | [Osilodrostat](/drugs/osilodrostat/) | The record gave the US indication as Cushing's disease only. On 15 April 2025 the FDA broadened it to endogenous hypercortisolaemia in adults with Cushing's syndrome for whom surgery is not an option or has not been curative. The record also said "most patients" reached normal cortisol in LINC 3; the label figure is 53% at 24 weeks without a dose increase. | FDA supplement approval letter for NDA 212801 S-003 (15 April 2025, read with pdftotext) and the US label of 18 November 2025 from openFDA, sections 1 and 14. | Approval row added for 2025, summary and one-line summary updated, and the LINC 3 figures (53% at 24 weeks; 86% against 29% in the randomised withdrawal period) stated from the label. |
| 2026-11-18 | [UroVysion Bladder Cancer Kit](/drugs/urovysion/) | The record said the FDA approved UroVysion in 2001 for monitoring bladder cancer recurrence. The 2001 decision was a 510(k) clearance (K011031, 3 August 2001, filed by Vysis), not an approval; the premarket approval came on 24 January 2005. The record also said the test is more sensitive than cytology "particularly for high-grade disease", which the meta-analysis read does not report. | FDA 510(k) and premarket approval records (K011031, P030052) from the openFDA device API; Hajdinjak 2008 meta-analysis (PubMed 18367109) abstract from Europe PMC. | Summary and approval rows now say cleared in 2001 and approved in 2005; sensitivity and specificity are given as the meta-analysis reports them (72% against 42%; 83% against 96%). The guideline sentence is marked as not re-verified. |
| 2026-11-18 | [Mitotane](/drugs/mitotane/) | The mechanism was stated as fact (conversion to an acyl chloride that binds mitochondrial proteins); the US label says the mechanism of action is unknown. The record called mitotane "the only drug specific to adrenal cortex cancer" and said it needs "permanent" steroid replacement, neither of which the label or the European product page says. The EU indication was given as "advanced adrenocortical carcinoma"; it is symptomatic treatment of advanced disease, with the effect on non-functional tumours not established. The US boxed warning for adrenal crisis was not mentioned. | US label (Lysodren, 3 March 2026) from openFDA, sections 1, 2.3, 5.1, 7.2 and 12.1 and the boxed warning; EMA product page for Lysodren read as raw HTML; Sbiera 2015 (PubMed 26305886) abstract from Europe PMC. | Mechanism now says what the label says and reports the SOAT1 finding as a laboratory study; the superlative and "permanent" are removed; the EU indication is given in full; the boxed warning and exact approval dates (8 July 1970; 28 April 2004) are added. |
| 2026-11-18 | [Olaratumab](/drugs/olaratumab/) | The record said Lilly withdrew the drug worldwide in 2019, and gave 2019 as the US withdrawal year. ### Second accuracy pass on drug records: sixteen more approved medicines and tests (slice 2, fifth batch), 18 November 2026

A second, independent read of 16 more records, among them ixazomib, aprepitant, the ArteraAI prostate test and hexaminolevulinate. 182 claims were checked: 12 were wrong, 20 were not supported by the source cited and 8 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: the ArteraAI prostate test was said to be cleared by the FDA to predict benefit from hormone therapy, where the clearance of 31 July 2025 covers prognosis only; the ixazomib record reported progression-free gains from two maintenance trials without the US label's warning of more deaths in both; and the aprepitant record said every guideline recommends three drugs for the most sickening chemotherapy, where ASCO and MASCC/ESMO recommend four.

The FDA's authorisation of 31 July 2025 covers prognosis only: 10-year risks of distant metastasis and of death from prostate cancer, in men aged 55 or older with non-metastatic disease. Predicting who benefits from hormone therapy is offered through the company's laboratory test and is not in the FDA's indication. | The FDA's granting letter for DEN240068, read with pdftotext, and the FDA de novo database entry. | The summary lines, the approval row, the regulatory event and the plain-language line now say what the FDA authorised and what it did not. |

### Second accuracy pass on drug records: forty-eight more approved medicines and tests (slice 2, fourth batch), 18 November 2026

A second, independent read of 48 more approved medicines and tests, from bosutinib, duvelisib and goserelin to pralatrexate, belinostat, isotretinoin and obecabtagene autoleucel. 651 claims were checked against labels, regulator pages, the trial registry and papers read as raw text: 50 were wrong, 43 were not supported by the source cited and 24 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: duvelisib was shown with an EU authorisation that was withdrawn in February 2026; belinostat's median duration of response was given as 10.8 months, which is its complete response rate in per cent; an isotretinoin finding in medulloblastoma was credited to a trial with no isotretinoin arm; romiplostim's trials in chemotherapy-induced low platelets were shown as under way after the phase 3 result was published in March 2026; elinzanetant's US and UK approvals were missing; and the PathVysion test was said to have been approved in 1998 to select trastuzumab, an indication added in 2001.

### Second accuracy pass on drug records: thirty-two more approved medicines (slice 2, third batch), 18 November 2026

A second, independent read of 32 more approved medicines and tests, from MammaPrint and orelabrutinib to lifileucel, panobinostat and sevabertinib. 533 claims were checked against labels, regulator pages, the trial registry and papers read as raw text: 38 were wrong, 30 were not supported by the source cited and 22 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: lifileucel was shown as approved in the EU in 2025, where the application was withdrawn in July 2025 and nothing was authorised; panobinostat's US withdrawal was dated 2021 in four places and read as worldwide, when the FDA withdrew approval in March 2022 and the EU authorisation stands; pexidartinib's EU application was shown as withdrawn by the company when the EMA refused it; estramustine was said to remain licensed in the United States, where the brand is discontinued, with a survival claim credited to a trial that never tested it; and sevabertinib was shown as unlicensed in the UK although the MHRA approved it in April 2026.

|---|---|---|---|---|

It also said the 8-year MINDACT update "showed a small benefit of chemotherapy in women under 50", when the paper calls that an underpowered exploratory analysis in women aged 50 or younger with a confidence interval that crosses zero, and it called the 2007 FDA clearance a 510(k) when the first clearance was through the de novo route. | The two MINDACT abstracts read as raw text from Europe PMC (PubMed 27557300 and 33721561) and the FDA device database read through openFDA (DEN070009, 6 February 2007; K070675, 22 June 2007). | TAILORx link removed. The summary now gives the paper's figures (2.6 points overall; 5.0 points in women aged 50 or younger, 95% CI -0.5 to 10.4; 0.2 points in older women), the approval row names the de novo clearance and its date, and the summary states that NICE (HTG719, May 2024) says the test should not be used to guide chemotherapy decisions. The NCCN listing is marked as not re-verified. |

### Second accuracy pass on drug records: thirty-two more approved medicines (slice 2, second batch), 18 November 2026

A second, independent read of 32 more approved medicines, from avapritinib and lapatinib to capmatinib, decitabine and idelalisib. 635 claims were checked against labels, regulator pages, the trial registry and papers read as raw text: 43 were wrong, 54 were not supported by the source cited and 28 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: relatlimab with nivolumab was said to have adjuvant trials under way, when RELATIVITY-098 found no benefit and was stopped; nirogacestat was shown as unlicensed and unfunded in the UK although the MHRA approved it in January 2026 and NICE recommended it in October 2026; the decitabine summary said its approval trial showed a delay in progression to leukaemia, which the label says it did not; capmatinib was still shown under accelerated approval, converted in August 2022; and FDG was called the first PET drug the FDA approved, when it was the third.

### Second accuracy pass on drug records: sixty-four approved medicines (slice 2, first batch), 18 November 2026

A second, independent read of 64 approved medicines, among them cisplatin, pemetrexed, nivolumab, atezolizumab, trastuzumab, enzalutamide, ibrutinib, tucatinib, selpercatinib, Pluvicto and teclistamab. Each claim was checked against the regulator's label or page, the trial registry or the paper, read as raw text. 1,518 claims were checked, of which 116 were wrong, 98 were not supported by the source cited and 59 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: the nivolumab summary said about half of people with advanced melanoma on nivolumab with ipilimumab are alive at ten years, where the ten-year paper gives a median survival of 71.9 months; the tucatinib dosing card predated the boxed liver warning added to the US label in October 2026; Pluvicto was shown as approved in the EU before chemotherapy, an application the company withdrew in March 2026; a US complete response letter was recorded for belantamab mafodotin that was never issued; the teclistamab dosing card gave the combination dose as the dose for the drug alone; and cobimetinib was shown as recommended by NICE and the SMC, which both declined it.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages: fourteen more high-burden cancers, 17 November 2026

The second group of high-burden cancers: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic, acute myeloid and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, oesophageal, kidney, endometrial and ovarian cancer, melanoma, glioblastoma, multiple myeloma, and the skin cancer family (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma with their treatment, living-with and UK layers). 2,189 ledger rows, of which 337 were wrong, 162 were not supported by the source cited and 116 could not be re-read. The most serious faults: odronextamab was shown as approved in the United States under another drug's brand name, when the regulator has twice declined it; niraparib was offered to a group its US label has excluded since March 2026; a melanoma page said half of patients with advanced disease live ten years, where the trial reports 43 per cent overall survival; first-line immunotherapy for oesophageal cancer was described as approved for all patients, where the current US labels require PD-L1 expression; and a gilteritinib trial after transplant (MORPHO) was written as positive although it missed its primary endpoint.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages: ten high-burden cancers, 17 November 2026

The second pass then moved to the cancers with the most cases in the GLOBOCAN data, one reader per cancer, covering the main record and its deeper file. This first group is non-small-cell and small-cell lung cancer, hormone receptor positive and HER2-positive breast cancer, head and neck, stomach, thyroid, liver, bladder and cervical cancer: 1,187 ledger rows, of which 244 were wrong, 71 were not supported by the source cited and 67 could not be re-read. Most of the wrong claims were out of date: approvals granted or indications removed during 2026 that the pages had not caught up with, trials described as pending after they had reported, and early survival results left standing after a later analysis. The most serious were a trial (HARMONi-3) recorded as having missed an interim analysis when the company's reports say only that it continues, an adjuvant breast cancer trial (APHINITY) said to show no survival benefit after its final analysis found one, and thyroid cancer care still written to a guideline replaced in 2025.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages: lymphoma, 17 November 2026

Lymphoma, twenty files and the records elsewhere that repeat their claims: 1,850 ledger rows, of which 220 were wrong, 140 were not supported by the source cited and 53 could not be re-read. This family has no generated registry file, so every row is a claim read against its source. The most serious faults were withdrawn treatments still shown as options and early results left standing: tazemetostat was offered for follicular lymphoma after its US approval was withdrawn on 22 June 2026, selinexor was offered for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after that indication was removed in April 2026, pixantrone was shown as funded in England after NICE withdrew its guidance, the H10 and LyMa gains were stated as settled although neither was significant at longer follow-up, and the address used for the US National Cancer Institute's lymphoma summary now opens a different summary from the one cited for aggressive and T-cell disease.

| Date | Entity | What was wrong | How found | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-11-17 | [Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (all types): share from B cells](/cancers/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/) | The summary line said about 95 percent of non-Hodgkin lymphoma comes from B cells. That figure, 94.7 percent, is the share of all lymphoma in the UK series, which counts Hodgkin lymphoma on the B-cell side. Among the 4,961 non-Hodgkin lymphomas in the series 308 were T-cell, which leaves 93.8 percent B-cell. The B-cell survival figure of 68.8 percent was also given without saying that group includes Hodgkin lymphoma | Second accuracy pass; the full text for DOI 10.1038/bjc.2015.94 read through Europe PMC | The summary line now says about 94 percent, and the passages that quote the series say it covers diagnoses from 2004 to 2012 and counts Hodgkin lymphoma with the B-cell lymphomas |
| 2026-11-17 | [Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (all types): staging, bulk and the E suffix](/cancers/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/) | Bulky disease was defined for every lymphoma as a mass of 10 cm or more or over a third of the chest width. The Lugano classification keeps that definition for Hodgkin lymphoma only and gives no validated size for non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The suffix E was described as a site reached by direct extension, leaving out a single extranodal site with no nodes involved | Second accuracy pass; the full text for DOI 10.1200/JCO.2013.54.8800 read as raw HTML from PubMed Central | The staging line gives the Hodgkin definition, the suggested sizes for follicular and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with the note that none is validated, and both meanings of E. The glossary entry on nodal and extranodal lymphoma carries the same wording |
| 2026-11-17 | [Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (all types): what causes death in follicular lymphoma](/cancers/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/) | Three passages said transformation is the commonest cause of death in follicular lymphoma, with no source. The pooled French and US analysis found lymphoma to be the leading cause of death, and 77 of the 140 deaths from lymphoma, out of 283 deaths in all, were in people whose disease had transformed | Second accuracy pass; the abstract for DOI 10.1200/JCO.18.00400 read through Europe PMC | The hub and the glossary entries on transformation and on indolent and aggressive lymphoma now give the 77 of 140 figure and link the paper |

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages: prostate cancer, 17 November 2026

Prostate cancer, eighteen files and the records elsewhere that repeat their claims: 2,322 ledger rows, of which 206 were wrong, 117 were not supported by the source cited and 40 could not be re-read. This cancer has no generated registry file, so every row is a claim read against its source. The most serious faults were early results left standing after the final analysis overturned them: DART 01/05 and RTOG 0521 were shown as survival gains although neither was significant at ten years, MAGNITUDE was said to show a survival benefit in BRCA carriers although its final analysis found none, and TRITON3 and IPATential150 were described without their non-significant final survival. Three PubMed ids in the UK layer opened unrelated papers, and the ERSPC screening trial was quoted only at its 2009 and 16-year figures after its 23-year report.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages: lung cancer, 17 November 2026

Lung cancer, seventeen files and the records elsewhere that repeat their claims: 2,575 ledger rows, of which 385 were wrong (187 of them registry records whose status, phase, sponsor, dates or enrolment had changed or were misdescribed), 108 were not supported by the source cited and 65 could not be re-read. The most serious faults were stale statuses and one reversed result: lurbinectedin was still shown as approved in the United States for relapsed small-cell lung cancer after that indication was removed from the label in September 2026; final overall survival for FLAURA2 was described as awaited after it was published; patritumab deruxtecan was offered as a later-line option after its US application was withdrawn; NICE guideline NG122 was cited by recommendation numbers that changed in November 2026; and the TIME2 trial of pleural catheters was described with its result the wrong way round.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages: colorectal cancer, 17 November 2026

Colorectal cancer, seventeen files and the records elsewhere that repeat their claims: 2,741 ledger rows, of which 578 were wrong (316 of them registry records whose status, phase, sponsor, dates or enrolment had changed or were misdescribed), 132 were not supported by the source cited and 45 could not be re-read. The most serious faults were stale statuses: adagrasib with cetuximab was shown as a current US approval for KRAS G12C disease in more than twenty places after the indication was removed from the label in August 2026; blood-test-guided escalation of chemotherapy was described as untested after DYNAMIC-III and ALTAIR had reported no benefit; and the NordICC colonoscopy trial was used as evidence that screening saves lives without saying its fall in deaths was not statistically significant.

| Date | Entity | What was wrong | How found | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-11-17 | [Colorectal cancer: NordICC and deaths from colorectal cancer](/cancers/colorectal/) | The screening paragraph, the screening question and the 2022 history row quoted NordICC's fall in cancer incidence as evidence that screening saves lives and did not say that its difference in deaths from colorectal cancer was not statistically significant (0.28 against 0.31 percent at 10 years, risk ratio 0.90, 95 percent confidence interval 0.64 to 1.16). ### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages: pancreatic cancer, 17 November 2026

Pancreatic cancer, seventeen files and the records elsewhere that repeat their claims: 1,908 ledger rows, of which 298 were wrong (149 of them registry records whose status, phase, sponsor, dates or enrolment had changed or were misdescribed), 78 were not supported by the source cited and 47 could not be re-read. The most serious faults were stale statuses: daraxonrasib was still described as an unapproved trial drug after its US approval on 26 August 2026, the SCALOP-2 trial was described as unpublished after it reported a negative result in 2024, MRTX1133 was listed as in development after its only trial was terminated, and a positive trial of treatment before surgery (Prep-02/JSAP05) was missing from every passage that said such treatment had shown no gain.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages: triple-negative breast cancer, 17 November 2026

Triple-negative breast cancer, eleven files and the records elsewhere that repeat their claims: 1,385 ledger rows, of which 198 were wrong (97 of them registry records whose status, dates, enrolment or interventions had changed or were misdescribed), 54 were not supported by the source cited and 27 could not be re-read. The most serious faults were results reported as still awaited (the NeoTRIP event-free survival analysis and the BARBICAN response rate, both negative), a registry link for CREATE-X that opened a different trial, and the PARTNER germline BRCA result credited to the paper that reported the negative main cohort.

### Second accuracy pass on the cancer pages: gallbladder cancer, 17 November 2026

The deep-dive cancer pages are being read a second time, claim by claim, by fresh readers with every cited source fetched again as raw text: trial results, approvals, guideline statements, survival and incidence figures, and every DOI, PubMed id and registry number. Gallbladder cancer, twelve files: 1,008 ledger rows, of which 148 were wrong (70 of them registry records whose status, dates or enrolment had changed or were misdescribed), 61 were not supported by the source cited and 39 could not be re-read. A row is one claim or one registry record. The most serious fault was a stale status: the ACTICCA-1 trial was described as awaited in six files after it had been published on 24 October 2026 without a significant gain in disease-free survival. Wrong and unsupported claims are corrected below; figures a reader would act on whose source could not be re-read are labelled on the record.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-11-17 | [Gallbladder cancer: adjuvant treatment](/cancers/gallbladder/) | The standard-of-care row said ACTICCA-1 "is awaited". The trial was published on 24 October 2026: gemcitabine and cisplatin did not significantly improve disease-free survival over capecitabine (median 25.7 against 17.9 months, log-rank P = 0.097) in 591 patients, 16 percent of them with gallbladder cancer. The 2019 history entry also called BILCAP the adjuvant standard without saying it missed its primary endpoint | Second accuracy pass; the abstract for pmid 42926109 (Annals of Oncology 2026) and the BILCAP abstract for DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(18)30915-X read through Europe PMC, and the registry record NCT02170090 | The row now gives the ACTICCA-1 result and says capecitabine stays the standard; the history entry gives the BILCAP intention-to-treat hazard ratio 0.81 (0.63 to 1.04) and says it was not statistically significant |

### Second accuracy pass on care protocols, 16 and 17 November 2026

The care protocols had one writer and a scripted check that each quotation appears in its source, and no independent re-read. This is a second check by a fresh reader of each protocol, with every cited source fetched again as raw text, taken in order of patient risk: emergencies first, then immunotherapy and cell-therapy toxicity, then protocols that carry drug doses. In all 226 protocols and 21,886 ledger rows: 816 wrong, 4117 not supported by the source cited (most often a step written as an order where the guideline says "consider", or a reason the source does not give), and 546 that could not be re-read because the source refused a script. A row is one checkable claim: a dose, a threshold, a quotation or a grade. Wrong and unsupported claims are corrected below; a claim whose source could not be re-read is named in the protocol's own list of gaps. Doses and figures that the checkers themselves added were then re-read by a second independent reader against the cited label or guideline; those corrections, the restored advice on when to seek urgent help, and the drug links removed are the rows marked as a re-read or follow-up.

### Institution records behind the country pages, 17 November 2026

The country accuracy passes checked each page's own text. This check went to the institution records those pages share: the hospitals on Newsweek's oncology list, the census of 83 smaller countries, and the records written with 97 country pages. 785 records were read against the sources they cite, with founding years, bed and machine counts, ranks, designations and every "only", "largest" and "first" taken first; long passages of policy were mostly not re-read. Of 1,728 ledger rows, 13 were wrong, 17 were not supported by the source cited, 26 could not be re-read and are now labelled or attributed on the record, and 21 had no address on the record, nearly all of which were confirmed in a primary source that is now linked. Second batch, same date. Four more countries (Ghana, Saudi Arabia, Peru and Nepal) bring the pass to sixteen, with 2,415 ledger rows: 49 wrong, 224 unsupported, 22 that could not be re-read and 90 with no address to test. Two faults recurred across pages and were corrected on all sixteen. Pages said the IAEA's radiotherapy directory (DIRAC) needed a sign-in or could not be read; its table loads from a public feed, which names each centre, its machines and the year of the entry, and the pages now say what it lists. And pages gave the lack of a registry as the reason IARC models a country's figures, which no source says; they now give WHO's or the review's dated statement and IARC's stated method as separate facts.

Third batch, same date. Nine more countries (Venezuela, Sri Lanka, Syria, Kazakhstan, Cambodia, Ecuador, Zimbabwe, Chile and Tunisia) bring the pass to twenty-five, with 3,807 ledger rows: 95 wrong, 352 unsupported, 29 that could not be re-read and 147 with no address to test. A third recurring fault was found and corrected on the earlier pages as well: HPV vaccination figures had been checked against a narrow query of WHO's immunisation data. The full set of rows shows that several headline figures are WHO's programme estimates, not coverage the country reported, and that the country's own administrative and official rows can differ widely (Sri Lanka's first-dose coverage in 2023 was given as 31% where the country reported 91.56%; Zimbabwe's 90% in 2025 sits beside 63% vaccinated by age 15; Ghana's 79% beside an administrative 0.57%). Pages now name the kind of figure and give both where they differ.

Fifth and last batch, same date. Seven more countries (Austria, Serbia, Denmark, Finland, Norway, Ireland and North Korea) complete the forty pages of waves 5 to 8, with 6,133 ledger rows in all: 184 wrong, 532 unsupported, 60 that could not be re-read and 217 with no address to test. That is 11.7 per cent of rows wrong or unsupported after one earlier check. The [statistics assessment](https://github.com/judegomila/OnCo/pull/375) retains five later-only lessons and their source-first requirements. They have no counterpart at the original pinned paths.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-11-12 | [Other-cause mortality](/terms/other-cause-mortality/) | The introduction inferred dependence from mutually exclusive events and conflated cumulative-incidence estimation with Fine-Gray regression | Austin's method definitions and the Therneau, Crowson and Atkinson vignette | Separates Aalen-Johansen probabilities, cause-specific rates and subdistribution hazards; replaces the single-cause explanation of disagreement between prostate trials without recertifying the retained prostate-cohort figures |
| 2026-11-12 | [Bayesian design](/terms/bayesian-trial-design/) and [response-adaptive randomisation](/terms/response-adaptive-randomisation/) | Leads implied a model-free probability that a treatment works and guaranteed efficiency or better assignments | Original I-SPY2 methods, complete primary abstracts, FDA's 2019 final guidance and January 2026 draft | States model, prior, endpoint, future-trial success criterion and operating-characteristic conditions; distinguishes predictive graduation, exploratory survival and a person's response-guided treatment path |

| 2026-11-12 | [Power and sample size](/terms/sample-size-re-estimation/) | Underpowering was called the commonest reason useful treatments fail and blinded re-estimation was said to have no statistical cost | ICH E9, adaptive-design guidance, CALOR methods and power-method sources | Replaces universal claims with specified effects, event information, planning assumptions and analysis requirements; independently checks the complete fictional calculations |
| 2026-11-12 | [Estimands](/terms/estimand/), [master protocols](/terms/master-protocol/) and [seamless designs](/terms/seamless-adaptive/) | Overviews conflated analysis sets with target effects and implied general patient-number or speed advantages | Targeted ICH E9(R1) and FDA guidance passages | Separates estimand, estimator and sensitivity analysis; makes efficiency conditional. Unverified clinical catalogues are withdrawn from these overviews with complete before/after fields retained in the packet and existing links preserved |

Every factual correction to the OnCo corpus, newest first. Format: date · entity · what was wrong · how it was found · fix.

## 2026-11-11

### Tumour immunology and experimental scope

- **Pathway maps:** removed claims that an inflamed pattern guarantees PD-1 response, that a class-I-loss tumour is automatically killed by NK cells, or that fixing one cancer-immunity-cycle step predicts cure. Antigen presentation, recognition, tissue access and useful killing remain separate dependencies. The beta-catenin recruitment example no longer combines PTEN loss with an unrelated PIK3CA target.
- **NK and antibody mechanisms:** the receptor map distinguishes activating and inhibitory inputs, education and measured function. Margetuximab is described as Fc-engineered, rather than grouped as an afucosylated antibody. Its label's receptor-binding and NK-activation findings retain their in-vitro scope. The negative INTERLINK-1 comparison is kept beside earlier laboratory findings. Sources: [Long et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23516982/), [MARGENZA label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=6a6d50c7-06ea-479c-83cc-f197a9e428c9), [INTERLINK-1](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40300079/).
- **Interferon and CD4 readouts:** impaired interferon inducibility is separated from loss of all baseline recognition. STAT1, STAT2, STAT3 and IRF1 retain the melanoma experiments' actual scope. A FOXP3 stain alone does not establish suppression, and CD4 includes experimentally demonstrated cytotoxic states. Sources: [Zaretsky et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27433843/), [Garcia-Diaz et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28494868/), [Tran et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17644734/), [Oh et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32497499/).
- **Spatial and clinical interpretation:** tumour-location labels, stromal-area scores and counted-cell fractions have different denominators. Pancreatic mouse mechanisms no longer establish a rule for all human pancreatic tumours or the only possible responder group. Perioperative biomarker findings, anaesthesia trial endpoints and combined local/systemic treatment effects retain their separate populations and comparison limits.

The [tumour-immunology checkpoint](https://github.com/judegomila/OnCo/pull/375) records both source inventories, exact draft fields and source-access limits. These additions do not certify every retained historical claim, expert review, a named-language translation or main/live publication.

## 2026-11-10

### Pneumonitis attribution and product-specific labels

- **Interruption and discontinuation:** replaced a single generic grade ladder with the named product's instructions. The May 2026 trastuzumab deruxtecan table retains its separate adjuvant radiotherapy-only footnote; datopotamab deruxtecan and the October 2026 pembrolizumab label retain their own confirmation, severity and resumption conditions.
- **Monitoring and incidence:** removed the unsupported scheduled-imaging requirement and universal workup. The warning sections specify symptom monitoring and prompt investigation, including imaging for suspected disease. Naidoo's incidence estimates retain their two-institution cohort, denominators and observational scope.

The [source and field checkpoint](https://github.com/judegomila/OnCo/pull/375) records the targeted reading, current-label check and validation. This corrects one record; it does not close the broader pharmacology and toxicity curriculum audit.

### Effect measures and evidence interpretation

- **Statistical interpretation:** corrected the lead-time superlative, the p-value probability gloss, an inverted absence-of-evidence sentence and unsupported hazard-ratio examples. Frequentist intervals, equivalence, non-inferiority, competing risks and survival clocks now retain their different questions and assumptions. Fictional calculations are labelled as such.
- **Endpoint source scope:** STEEP 2.0's actual table distinguishes distant RFI from distant relapse-free survival. Aalen-Johansen is attributed to the reviewed technical vignette, separately from Austin's competing-risk tutorial. FDA endpoint guidance retains its December 2018, nonbinding scope. IDFS's existing check date is unchanged.
- **Surrogate examples:** corrected the historical olaratumab approval rationale and scoped the named trial comparisons. The TROPION-Breast01 account includes later antibody-drug-conjugate use. Unchecked legacy CodeBreaK 200, adjuvant-endpoint, MRD and UKCTOCS assertions are deliberately withdrawn from the summary and retained as named source follow-ups; related-study links remain.
- **Reader text and citations:** consolidated this batch's repeated notes while preserving published notes and unique source-backed teaching. Clinical benefit, assay signals, model outputs and personal predictions remain separate. DOI-cache additions record only individually resolved identifiers and preserve the broader cache date.

Source versions, exact fields, independent review findings and remaining work are recorded in the [statistics checkpoint](https://github.com/judegomila/OnCo/pull/375).

### Dose changes and CRS grading

- **Dose modification:** removed unsourced class-wide dose-reduction and discontinuation ranges, a universal 85% dose-intensity claim, and an implication that lower targeted-drug doses are generally equivalent. The record now defines its reference and time basis, gives labelled fictional arithmetic, and scopes the Zhang observational and Goetz exploratory analyses to their populations. Eight stale short translations use current English fallback; the accurate simple definition is retained. Sources: [Alberto, 1995](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7626852/), [Zhang et al., 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29368311/), [Goetz et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41523-024-00639-1).
- **CRS grading:** the lymphoma record described grade 2 hypotension as responding to fluids. The 2019 consensus uses hypotension not requiring vasopressors. The correction preserves the vasopressin exceptions, oxygen-support criteria and the rule that subsequent grading can proceed without fever after treatment of established CRS. Other management and trial text is carried forward outside this focused verification. Source: [Lee et al., original consensus author manuscript, Table 2 and footnotes](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12180426/).

### Binder evidence and manufacturing quality

- **Cell-product identity and release:** an older definition and summary presented HLA identity and a generic rapid-sterility timeline as a release checklist. They now distinguish engineered-cell identity, chain of identity, viability, potency and product-specific testing. FDA's scoped 2020 short-shelf-life example does not become a universal early-release rule. Corrected short translations already present in the shared draft are preserved with the aligned English definition.
- **Peptide benchmark and vaccine regimen:** the 29-peptide Truex vendor comparison used deliberately difficult sequences. The Rojas study gave vaccine and atezolizumab to sixteen recipients, followed by chemotherapy in fifteen; the observed response is not attributed to vaccine alone.
- **Binder comparison scope:** Kinna's thermal and particle measurements are separated from predicted aggregation scores. Its xenograft used a human AML cell line in mice, and its single-donor limitation concerns preceding cell work. Single-domain shark binding fragments are distinguished from the full receptor.
- **Guidance identity:** FDA's final November 2026 potency guidance has a different landing URL from the retained December 2023 draft page. The final PDF and 3 November Federal Register notice support the current text; a content-current date is not treated as an issuance day. US manufacturer release and conditional official FDA lot release retain their separate scopes.

Exact fields, source identities and read-depth limits are retained in the [binder and manufacturing checkpoint](https://github.com/judegomila/OnCo/pull/375).

### Innate immunity, cell identity and source scope

- **Macrophage states:** the retained TAM summary treated an M2-like label as the prevailing identity. It now explains that M1/M2 labels arise from laboratory stimulation and do not certify a tumour cell's state or suppressive function. The location name, measured programme and functional test remain separate. Sources and exact fields are in the [innate source reconciliation](https://github.com/judegomila/OnCo/pull/375).
- **Recognition systems:** the immune-system definition replaces a rigid fast/generic versus slow/remembering division with inherited receptor systems versus receptors assembled during development, while preserving qualified trained-monocyte and memory-like NK findings. Chemokine activation effects and soluble complement defences are explicit rather than lost in the comparison.
- **Experimental scope:** the checkpoint additions keep the galectin-9/Bat3 binding result in the tested 293T setting, separate from the Th1-cell death result. The reviewed receptor-selection article is described as a review. Interferon protein amount, RNA score and controlled-exposure activity retain distinct readouts; receptor-family labels do not measure dose or potency.
- **Glossary routing:** singular and plural interferon lookup now belong to the dedicated interferon-family term; the broad cytokine definition remains linked. No ambiguous DCs alias is added.

### Breast anatomy, pathology and source scope

- **Ki-67 and monarchE:** the retained summary attributed the 20% eligibility threshold to cohort 1. It belonged to cohort 2; cohort 1 used its specified node, grade and size criteria. The current note separates trial eligibility from the FDA's 2023 removal of the testing requirement. MIB-1 remains a named assay antibody, rather than the definition of every Ki-67 index. Source: [FDA abemaciclib expansion](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-information-approved-drugs/fda-expands-early-breast-cancer-indication-abemaciclib-endocrine-therapy).
- **p63 denominator:** the Werling series reported at least focal tumour-cell staining in 11% of cases, rather than staining in 11% of tumour cells. Cohort-specific observations are not universal diagnostic accuracy. Source: [Werling et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12502930/).
- **Response definitions:** pCR is tied to its named specimens and endpoint. The FDA's two combined breast-and-node trial definitions differ on residual DCIS, while older studies also used breast-only endpoints. RCB retains protocol-specific tumour-bed and nodal measurements, its empirically fitted equation and class cutoffs; fictional equation arithmetic does not certify a calculator response or an individual recurrence probability. Sources: [FDA pCR guidance](https://www.fda.gov/media/83507/download), [Symmans et al.](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2007.10.6823).
- **Grading and staging:** CAP grade fields retain their applicability conditions. Accessible raw RCPath G148 text supports the restored source-specific reporting and audit statements. Its UICC-versus-AJCC instruction is no longer stretched into a rule that all UK reports omit prognostic staging. The audit's earlier source-access failure was not reproducible.
- **Clinical comparison scope:** breast-conservation trials found no significant survival difference in eligible study populations; they did not prove exactly equal personal survival probabilities. TAM-01 compared low-dose tamoxifen with placebo, and COMET's monitoring result concerns selected low-risk DCIS and short follow-up. B-51's nodal-irradiation result is tied to its cT1 to T3, cN1, M0 to ypN0 population. Sources: [long-term surgery comparison](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12393819/), [TAM-01](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.22.02900), [COMET](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2024.26698), [B-51](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2414859).
- **Reader preservation:** source-backed anatomy, sampling and treatment context is restored with its qualifications. Forty-six stale short summaries now use current English fallback; existing unaffected text and review labels remain. The Spanish and Chinese full pCR examples are refreshed against the current English hash and attributed as model drafts. No new named language review is claimed.

### Sequencing, RNA measurements and updated TMB policy

- **TMB selection:** current tumour-agnostic pembrolizumab statements now use the FDA October 2026 traditional-approval criterion of at least 13 mutations per megabase, with the authorised-test, disease and treatment-setting conditions. The former 10-mut/Mb criterion and published study cutoffs retain their historical scope; no response guarantee or universal low-TMB contraindication is inferred. Sources: [FDA conversion and updated indication](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/cancer-approvals/fda-grants-traditional-approval-pembrolizumab-or-pembrolizumab-and-berahyaluronidase-alfa-pmph), [current KEYTRUDA label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=9333c79b-d487-4538-a9f0-71b91a02b287).
- **What sequencing establishes:** read count, independent molecules, local depth, breadth, mutation density, cell purity and inferred cancer-cell fraction keep their own denominators and assumptions. Tumour-only sequencing does not establish constitutional origin from a familiar gene or allele fraction. Sources include [Jones et al.](https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.aaa7161) and [the TMB harmonisation experiment](https://doi.org/10.1136/jitc-2019-000147). Numerical exercises are fictional, not clinical thresholds.
- **HLA source scope:** the [LOHHLA study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2017.10.001) selected all-loci-loss or no-loss regions for a validation comparison; that selection does not establish typical regional frequency. Gene-specific HLA locations are verified against HGNC. DNA retention, RNA expression, surface protein and peptide display remain distinct findings.
- **RNA readers:** captured RNA, probe counts, expression scores, inferred mixture components and functional output retain their separate methods. Reverse transcription is a common workflow rather than a definition of every RNA chemistry. Sixty-three stale short summaries use current English fallback, while 47 unchanged short entries retain their text and positions; no new named language review is claimed.

### Spatial methods and model evaluation

- **Model evaluation:** a held-out 80/20 split is no longer described as a universal minimum. Internal, external, donor and intervention holdouts answer different questions, and choices made using evaluation results become part of development. Sources include [TRIPOD+AI](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-078378) and the [single-cell perturbation benchmark](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02772-6).
- **Protein measurements:** mass spectrometry does not measure every protein or directly establish cellular function, and it is not an exclusive route to phosphorylation information. Protein-derived peptides, phosphosite signals, model estimates, cell assignments and functional effects retain their own scopes. Sources include the [protein-inference methods paper](https://doi.org/10.1021/pr401072g) and the [breast proteogenomic study](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature18003).
- **Predictions and assays:** unqualified transfer and clinical-response claims are removed from inherited lead paragraphs. A virtual-cell model returning no response to a mutation-driven drug is not guaranteed to be correct. The [IC50-to-Ki methods paper](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkp253) supports the assay-condition distinction; an unverified FFPE immunopeptidomics adaptation is explicitly withheld. Existing notes carry the worked examples and reading guides, and four stale short summaries use current English fallback without a new language-review claim.


### Repair, signalling and what the assays establish

- **MYC citation:** the inherited link labelled OMO-103 resolved to a glioma CAR-T trial. The DOI is corrected to the independently resolved [Garralda phase 1 OMO-103 study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-024-02805-1), already represented by the existing paper owner. No clinical benefit is inferred from MYC abundance.
- **Repair:** the short definitions no longer equate a variant, a genomic scar or a damage signal with current repair failure or treatment eligibility. Classical end joining is not described as universally inaccurate, and paired repair disruptions are not described as universally lethal. The [original LST study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22933060/), [Telli study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26957554/) and [selected resistance cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32245699/) retain their own methods, populations and endpoints.
- **Signalling:** receptor amount, phosphorylation, drug engagement, functional dependence and clinical benefit have distinct interpretations. The [RAF transactivation experiment](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20179705/) and [WNT974 phase 1 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33941878/) are scoped to their actual interventions and observations. The existing KEAP1 identity receives a handwritten override through the established generated-target precedence rule, preserving its catalogue fields and lung supplement; generated gene files are unchanged.
- **Source and reader boundaries:** the crosslink-repair review is labelled as a review. DNA-fiber calibration and numerical practice examples are explicitly protocol-specific or fictional. Unscoped legacy prevalence, treatment, price and turnaround assertions are replaced by the completed source-scoped explanations; a clinical landscape update is a separate queued task. Stale short translations use the current English fallback and receive no new language-review claim.

### RNA design, delivery and evidence boundaries

- **AAV:** the source audit distinguishes a named viral genome, packaged-genome measurements and usable coding capacity. A general self-complementary capacity figure is replaced with the original inverted-repeat experiment and its coding-capacity trade-off. The blanket claim that none of the cited studies concerns cancer is corrected: the T-cell editing study includes a mouse leukaemia model, while human cancer benefit is not established here. Sources include [McCarty 2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11509958/), [McCarty 2008](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18682697/) and [Eyquem](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28225754/).
- **RNA carriers and constructs:** ionisable-lipid charge is qualified by lipid and environment. Entry, endosomal release, expression, integration, receptor recognition and useful activity retain their own assays and populations. A residual-DNA number from a review is not treated as a universal release specification; the [NEB IVT protocol](https://www.neb.com/en-us/protocols/evaluation-of-ivt-reaction-products?pdf=true) supplies the explicitly vendor-scoped UV measurement caveat.
- **Coverage and ownership:** repeated takeaways and source lists retain dispositions without earning extra teaching credit. The assertion that on-target/off-tumour toxicity had no owner is corrected after finding existing therapeutic-index and lineage-antigen aliases. Their broader class-safety claims remain queued for verification rather than being inherited as fact.

### Evidence interpretation and worked examples

- **Absence of evidence:** corrected an inverted double negative. A documented search without an exact-variant drug-response report establishes neither resistance nor benefit. Nonsignificance, equivalence and non-inferiority retain their distinct hypotheses, assumptions and margins.
- **Measurements and transport:** connected notes now distinguish variant evidence, pathway signals, dependence, engagement and clinical outcomes; tumour-volume examples retain their different scope from cell-assay growth-rate metrics and RECIST. Trial eligibility, transport assumptions and individual prediction remain separate. Repeated batch examples are consolidated without dropping unique teaching or earlier links.
- **Source identity:** newly cached DOIs were individually resolved. The shared cache date is preserved; it does not claim every citation was freshly checked.

### Immunogenicity and clinical efficacy

- **Exercise scope:** the linked fictional exercise supplies a receptor-repertoire change alongside a tumour-DNA result. It does not supply a tumour sequence match or a positive peptide test. The corrected account separates specificity, function, attribution and detection limits without adding those facts.
- **Evidence boundaries:** connected notes retain assay preparation, natural tumour recognition, clinical comparisons, harms and uncertainty. An immune result can justify further investigation without settling added clinical benefit. Repeated batch material is consolidated; existing links remain. A newly cached DOI was individually resolved without updating the broader cache date.

## 2026-11-09

### Cell death, stress and source-review corrections

- **Cell-death mechanisms:** apoptosis no longer owns the broad aliases “cell death” or “programmed cell death”. The assessed records distinguish mitochondrial/death-receptor routes, necrotic appearance, durable senescence and adaptive immune consequences. Immunogenic markers alone do not establish useful immunity; [consensus assay guidance](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32209603/) retains that boundary.
- **Autophagy, ferroptosis and metabolism:** descriptions now keep assay, model and perturbation limits. They no longer turn a selected cell-state dependency into a universal cancer property or a metabolic perturbation into clinical benefit. [Horton’s transgenic comparison](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9616204/) separates SREBP-relative effects and measured synthesis; [Freed-Pastor’s 3D cultures](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22265415/) retain the nonsterol rescue distinction. Oxygen-consumption calculations now name the [published ATP-rate correction](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30097494/).
- **Antibody, HLA, tertiary lymphoid structures and TAP:** independent source review found three overcredited requirements, an omitted scoped association, duplicated TLS prose and an imprecise TAP citation label. Exact fields now state that same-target antibody formats can differ, distinguish ectopic location from a developmental stage, retain the scope of breast/melanoma associations and identify the TAP1 experiment. The [primary HLA comparison](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25754738/) keeps its specific haplotype and method dependence.


### Antigen presentation, antibody functions and gene definitions

- **Antibody, epitope, B cell, ADCC, Fc function and HLA typing:** the sixteen-lesson audit separates receptor binding, display, activation and completed function; removes antibody-format and Fc-silencing generalisations; and prevents broad HLA names from standing in for a resolved allele. Stale short-summary entries now use corrected English fallback.
- **B2M, HLA and Fc-receptor genes:** short definitions describe checked protein functions rather than treating cancer-catalogue roles as definitions of normal growth control. Dated catalogue assertions retain their original scope. The remaining generator/corpus issue is explicitly queued.
- **HLA-C:** the observed peptide share retains the cell-line and assignment-method limits reported by [Schellens and colleagues](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26375851/), alongside [allele-dependent expression](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28649982/). This audit does not establish a universal peptide fraction or clinical response rule.

### T-cell identity and exhaustion

- **T cell and T-cell exhaustion pathway:** the generic T-cell definition implied universal target recognition and killing, and the exhaustion description used absolute rescue and DNA-fixation wording. The 14-page public education audit separated identity, recognition, state, measured function and benefit; it also removed subset/state aliases from the generic owner and placed true aliases on the specific terms. Primary sources include [human class-II-dependent CD4 cytotoxicity](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32497499/), [distinct exhaustion programmes](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17950003/), [different exhausted subsets](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30778252/), [chromatin stability after blockade](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27789795/) and [human clonal replacement](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31359002/). Twenty-seven translated/simplified entries now preserve these limits. This is an automated source audit, not expert or fluent-language sign-off. The existing detailed intervention maps retain a separately queued evidence review.

### Second accuracy pass on live country pages, waves 9 to 12

Every factual claim on the country pages of waves 9 to 12 is being read a second time against its cited source, fetched as raw text on 16 November 2026, one fresh checker per country. Each claim has a verdict in a ledger: supported, wrong, unsupported by the cited source, or unverifiable because the source did not answer that day. | 2026-11-08 | [Accelerated approval](/terms/accelerated-approval/) | Generalized example-based withdrawal language without retaining indication and regulatory-process context | FDA accelerated-approval program and expedited-program guidance | Retains indication-specific confirmation and applicable withdrawal procedures |
| 2026-11-08 | [Research use only](/terms/research-use-only/) | Generalized IVD guidance into legal requirements for every research model and website | FDA RUO/IUO guidance | Scopes the category to applicable intended-use and distribution rules |
| 2026-11-08 | [LDT rule](/terms/fda-ldt-rule/) | Assigned all LDT clinical claims one FDA-review status | Current FDA vacatur/restoration notice and CMS laboratory-quality materials | Separates test origin, laboratory oversight, product authorization and clinical evidence |
| 2026-11-08 | [Marketing applications](/terms/bla-nda/) | Called the review target a deadline with a promised decision and generalized application timing | FDA NDA, BLA, IND and expedited-program information | Separates submission, filing, review goals and approval |
| 2026-11-08 | [Expanded access](/terms/expanded-access/) | Gave a general review-time shortcut and omitted the new-IND versus existing-IND protocol distinction | FDA expanded-access questions and answers, April 2026, Q4 to Q9 | Adds route-specific criteria, calendar versus working-day rules, review duties and separate delivery dependencies |

## 2026-11-03

### Accuracy round 2: a census of the country pages and the 60 most-linked cancer pages

Every numeric or dated sentence on the live country pages (United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Israel, India, Japan, Russia, China and the research-ranking context file) and every figure-bearing sentence on the 60 cancer pages with the most inbound links was read against its cited source in raw text: 3,875 sentences, 3,402 with a checkable figure. Before these fixes 25.0 percent of country figures [23.1 to 27.1] and 20.8 percent of cancer-page figures [18.8 to 22.8] were wrong, stale, imprecise or had no source on the page; 4.2 and 1.2 percent were plainly wrong. Verdicts are in `docs/audits/accuracy/sample-2026-11-03-round2-sweep.json` and the rates in `ledger.json`. Where a fault recurred, every copy in the corpus was found and fixed, and four checks now hold the line: `src/data/burden-dated.test.ts`, `src/data/burden-sourced.test.ts`, `src/data/country-extras.test.ts` and `scripts/doi-exists.test.ts`.

## How corrections are logged

- Anyone can report an error via a GitHub issue or pull request.
- A correction entry names the entity, states precisely what was wrong, says how it was found (reader report, automated audit, fact-check job, congress update, reviewer), and links the fixing commit.
- The automated [audit](/audit/) and weekly registry fact-check surface candidates; only confirmed errors are logged here.

## Surface-targeting evidence and labels, 11 November 2026

The [surface-targeting correction record](https://github.com/judegomila/OnCo/pull/375) qualifies target/dependence, processing, PK and target-ranking claims. It corrects the SG human-serum release value against the 2020 notice, IDeate-Lung02 outcome hierarchy and the displayed tarlatamab cycle-1 schedule/monitoring. Source-specific assays, cohorts and model results replace universal safety, resistance and superiority assertions. All prior notes and source links remain in order; broader catalogue and mechanism-template gaps remain explicit.

The [current-main refresh](https://github.com/judegomila/OnCo/pull/375) retains upstream irAE aliases and makes the immune-side-effect lead name its organ examples and conditional management, supported by the label and prior guideline assessment. It does not change search ranking or its floors.

### Mesothelin healthy-tissue risk, 12 November 2026

Removed the inference that a presumed dispensable protein function means little risk from targeting mesothelin on healthy tissue. Normal mesothelial expression requires functional testing of the actual binder and engineered product; a positive tumour stain does not establish safety. The Tchou tissue survey and live-cell experiment retain their separate populations. Sources: [Tchou et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22418702/), [FDA CAR T-cell development guidance](https://www.fda.gov/media/156896/download).

### Cell-therapy time short summaries, 12 November 2026

Removed the unsupported typical three-to-six-week range from the vein-to-vein short lead and its simple-English entry. The same inherited clause was removed from the eight translated short definitions while preserving their existing definition wording. The interval and analysis population depend on the programme; manufacture, transport, testing and clinical readiness are different parts of the pathway. This is a source-scope correction, with no native-language review claimed. Source: [FDA CAR T-cell development guidance](https://www.fda.gov/media/156896/download).
